title: 50 m hurdles, free-standing hurdles
rulebook: World Athletics Competition and Technical Rules, 2024 edition: TR 22 (22.1-22.3 distances and heights: the men's hurdle 1.067 m high, 13.72 m to the first, 9.14 m between; at the indoor distance of 50 m that is four hurdles and 8.86 m from the last to the finish; 22.4-22.5 the hurdle: metal with a non-metallic top bar, two bases and two uprights at the extreme end of each base supporting a rectangular frame reinforced by a cross bar, 1.18 to 1.20 m wide, a top bar 70 mm high and 10 to 25 mm thick, a base at most 0.70 m long, at least 10 kg, counterweights set so that a horizontal force of 3.6 to 4.0 kg at the centre of the top bar's top edge topples it; placed with the feet towards the approaching athlete; 22.6 each hurdle is gone over in the athlete's own lane; 22.6.1 a foot or leg beside the hurdle below the plane of its top; 22.6.2 knocking down or displacing a hurdle by hand or body; 22.7 knocking hurdles down otherwise is no offence), TR 17.3 (lanes), TR 18.2 and TR 19 (the finish)
deviations: TR 16 (the start): no starter's commands, no blocks and no reaction time: the robot stands with the front ends of its feet 0.02 m behind the start line and the clock runs from t = 0

TR 22.6 ('goes over each hurdle') is judged geometrically at the hurdle's standing pose on its mark, wherever the hurdle is now: the pelvis must pass above the height of the hurdle's top, each foot (its ankle joint) above the lower edge of the top bar, all three between the bar's ends, through the plane where the top bar stood, all three in one flight (from the first crossing to the last the robot touches nothing but that hurdle's top bar: the rule book's clearance is a stride in the air, and a leg swung over from the ground or a step over a hurdle that lies on the track is not one); a hurdle that has fallen, or has been pushed on or out of the lane, does not lower or move what is to be gone over; going over it on the hurdle (climbing) is judged by contact: a hurdle not yet gone over that still stands may not push the robot upwards by more than 100.0 N for longer than 0.15 s, and at the instant the pelvis or a foot crosses its plane only the legs may touch it, on its top bar

TR 22.6.2 (knocking down or displacing a hurdle by hand, body or the upper side of the lead leg) and TR 22.7: intent and the side of the leg cannot be judged, so the cause of a hurdle's displacement is judged from contacts: a hurdle that leaves its standing pose (a point of its top bar more than 0.1 m from where it stood) within 0.5 s of a touch by a hand, an arm, the trunk or the pelvis is a failure if that touch was the robot's latest on it or came within 0.1 s; the legs may knock it down, on its top bar, during the clearance (while the robot touches nothing but that hurdle's top bar, or its pelvis is over the hurdle's plane); any other displacement before the hurdle is gone over (pushed, kicked or shoved along the track first, from the ground) is a failure: the athlete did not go over that hurdle as it stood

TR 17.3 (lanes): the lane is judged by the pelvis (its centre more than half a lane width from the lane's centre line); TR 22.6.1 is judged on the centres of the legs' collision bodies within 0.1 m of the hurdle's plane
TR 17 (a fallen athlete): a robot whose pelvis is below 0.4 m is down; it may get up and go on, but 10.0 s down in a row end the race (did not finish)

TR 19 (photo finish): the time is the instant the leading point of the torso link's collision mesh reaches the finish line's plane, interpolated between 1 ms physics steps (the H1-2's trunk and head are one link, so its torso includes the head); no wind; the robot alone on a straight of three lanes

TR 22.4-22.5 (the hurdle): a rigid body (no deflection of the top bar); the rule book does not give the friction of a hurdle on the track: 0.6 (rubber feet on a polyurethane track); the counterweights are set once for the toppling force 3.8 kg; the distance is the indoor 50 m with its four hurdles, on an outdoor straight, not the 110 m; the time limit, 140 s, is this benchmark's (FAMILIES.md)

texts.sentence: Run the 50 m hurdles over four free-standing hurdles: go over each one in your lane, never beside it, under its top, or after pushing it away, and bring your torso to the finish line.
texts.rules: World Athletics rules for the hurdles, at the indoor distance of 50 m. The lane runs along +x, 1.22 m wide, centred on y = 0; the start line (0.05 m wide) has its far edge at x = 0, the finish line is x = 50.0 m. 4 hurdles stand across the lane, the face of the first one's top bar 13.72 m from the start line and one every 9.14 m after it (the last 8.86 m before the finish). A hurdle is a loose object standing on the track: 1.19 m wide and 1.067 m high, a top bar 0.07 m high, two uprights and a cross bar 0.35 m below its top; its two bases, 0.7 m long, lie on the track on your side of it, with counterweights on them; it weighs 10.9 kg and tips over forwards when a horizontal force of more than 3.8 kg pushes the middle of its top bar (tipped further than about 55 degrees it falls on by itself); it can slide on the track (friction 0.6), fall, bounce and lie where it comes to rest, and you can trip on it, but not climb on it. Each hurdle is judged where it stands at the start (its standing pose on its mark), wherever it is later. The clock starts at t = 0. You go over a hurdle when your pelvis and both your feet (the ankle joints) have crossed the plane of its top bar in its standing pose towards +x, each between the bar's two ends, the pelvis higher than the hurdle's top (1.067 m above the track) and each foot higher than the lower edge of its top bar (1.067 m less 0.07 m), whether the hurdle still stands there or not, and in one flight: from the first of these three crossings to the last, no part of you touches anything but that hurdle's top bar; a pelvis or a foot that comes back over the plane has not crossed it and must cross it again. The hurdles are gone over in order. A hurdle leaves its standing pose when a point of its top bar is more than 0.1 m from where it stood. Knocking a hurdle down with your legs is allowed when a leg strikes its top bar during the clearance: while you touch nothing else but that hurdle's top bar (in the air) or once your pelvis is over the hurdle's plane; a hurdle tipped more than 60.0 degrees is counted as down, without a fault. Where a hurdle comes to rest after that does not matter. You finish at the moment the leading point of your torso (the trunk and head hull; not the arms, legs or feet) reaches the finish line, with all hurdles gone over. You succeed with a finish within 140 s of robot time. A fall does not end the race: you are down while your pelvis is below 0.4 m, you may get up and go on, but 10.0 s down in a row end it. You fail if your pelvis or a foot crosses the next hurdle's plane beside the hurdle, or lower than said above (going under its top); if between the first and the last of these crossings you touch the track or anything else but its top bar (stepping over it); if a part of one of your legs is beside the next hurdle (beyond the bar's ends, within 0.1 m of its plane) lower than the hurdle's top; if a hurdle leaves its standing pose within 0.5 s of being touched by a hand, an arm, your trunk or your pelvis, that touch being your latest on it or within 0.1 s before (knocked by hand or body; also one you have gone over); if you climb on a hurdle you have not yet gone over while it stands (tipped less than 60.0 degrees): it pushes you upwards by more than 100.0 N for longer than 0.15 s, or anything of you but a leg on its top bar touches it at the instant your pelvis or a foot crosses its plane; if a hurdle you have not yet gone over leaves its standing pose in any other way than the legal knock above (pushed, kicked or shoved along the track before you went over it); if your pelvis is more than half the lane's width from y = 0; if your torso reaches the finish line before every hurdle is gone over; when down for 10.0 s; or after 140 s.
texts.venue: You stand in your lane facing the finish (+x), the front ends of your feet 0.02 m behind the start line, your pelvis 0.23 m behind it. The lane lines are white on a red track; the hurdles' top bars are white with black stripes, their bases and counterweights grey on the track, reaching 0.7 m towards you along the lane's edges; two white posts stand beside the finish line. In your rest pose your forearms point forward at about the height of a hurdle's top.
texts.difficulty: A hurdle's top is higher than the robot's hip joints: each of the four has to be jumped with the whole pelvis above 1.067 m and each foot lifted a metre, on a body of 67 kg whose only built-in gait walks at 0.7 m/s and drifts in heading. The hurdles are loose: a clipped bar tips one into the landing, where it lies as an obstacle, and walking up to one shoves it away, which is a failure.

stand.meaning: the platform holds the legs in the stance; you give the waist's 1 and the arms' 14 joint targets (rad)

walk.meaning: Unitree's walking policy drives the legs from the velocity command (vx forward, vy to the left, m/s; wz turning left, rad/s; the robot's own frame); you give the waist and arm joint targets

joints.meaning: you give all 27 joint targets (rad); the default PD gains, no feed-forward

lowcmd.meaning: Unitree's LowCmd for all 27 joints: position targets (rad), velocity targets (rad/s), feed-forward torques (N m), kp, kd; the motor torque is kp (q - q_measured) + kd (dq - dq_measured) + tau, evaluated at 1 kHz

grip.rule: a closed grip holds the nearest grippable object whose surface is within reach_m of the palm (a point 4.5 cm beyond the wrist flange along the forearm) and that moves no faster than max_relative_speed_m_s relative to it; opening the grip lets it go
